name: Leo the Philosopher
bio: Leo the Philosopher is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to Byzantine period. Paton's index describes him as Byzantine.
This archive carries the 7 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 200, 201, 202, 214, 361, 578, 579).

poems.title: Book IX, 200
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: The book of mechanics, the work of Cyrinus, his friend Marcellus participating in the task.

poems.title: Book IX, 201
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: Paulus, famous among the astrologers, instructed me in the divine mysteries of Phoebus’ prophetic art.

poems.title: Book IX, 202
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: The book of Theo and Proclus the all-wise. The book exhibits the measurements of the Heavens and the Earth. Theo measures the Heavens and Proclus the Earth, or rather Proclus measures the Earth and Theo the Heavens. Both are worthy of equal praise, and both of them gave and took their respective arguments; for Theo, assuming the learned propositions of Proclus, demonstrates by these the courses of the stars; while Proclus, assuming the demonstrations of Theo, resolves and propounds his positions by their aid. All hail, learned pair! Hail, most excellent Theo, learned in every science, now adorning the city of Alexandria! And thou too, Proclus, hail, last scion of the race of Sarpedon and universally acclaimed !

poems.title: Book IX, 214
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: Porphyry, with the purple of thy discourse thou dyest the lips and clothest the mind in splendour.

poems.title: Book IX, 361: A Homeric Cento
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: My cruel-hearted mother, an evil mother to me— it pains me much, the wound that a mortal man inflicted on me—in the dark night when other mortals sleep—naked, without a helmet and shield, nor had he a spear—and all his sword was bathed in hot blood—but afterwards he sent forth a gentle and harmless gale.

poems.title: Book IX, 578: On the Conic Sections of Apollonius
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: Deep, reader, and exceeding hard is the character of the things wherewith this book is big, and it has every need of a Delian diver. But if one dive into its depths and investigate accurately every recess, he shall gain the first prize in geometry, and be pronounced indisputably a learned man. Plato is witness and security for this.

poems.title: Book IX, 579
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: Look, Corinthian founder of Sicily, who once didst drink the famous waters of Syracusan Arethusa, upon the herald’s staff as shaped by men of old time.’

poems.title: Book XV, 12
poems.author: Leo the Philosopher
poems.text: Thou art kind to me, Fortune, in adorning me with the most sweet restfulness of Epicurus and giving me calm to enjoy it. What need have I of men’s activity with all its cares? I desire not wealth, a blind and inconstant friend, nor honours, for the honours of mortals are a feeble dream. Away with thee, murky den of Circe, for I am ashamed, being of heavenly origin, to eat acorns like a beast. I hate the sweet food of the Lotus-eaters that causes men to abandon their country. I reject as my enemy the seductive music of the Sirens, but I pray to gain from God the flower that saves the soul, moly that protects from evil doctrines, and stopping my ears securely with wax may I escape the ill inborn impulse. Thus speaking and thus writing may I reach the end of my days.
